Dan Ashworth, United’s sporting director, said: “Signing Manuel was another of our primary targets for this summer. We wanted more energy, more aggression and more control in the centre of the pitch. Manuel brings all of that, as well as a mentality that fits what we are building here.”

Ashworth explained that United’s recruitment team had tracked the Uruguayan since his early days in South America. “We have followed his progress over several years,” he added. “Every time he stepped up a level, he adapted quickly. That gave us strong belief that he can handle the demands at this club. His character references were outstanding, and when we spoke to him directly it was clear he was hungry to grow and to compete for major honours.”

Erik ten Hag, who had pushed for an additional holding midfielder, was equally enthusiastic. The manager regards Ugarte as central to his plan to add more intensity and resilience in front of the back line. Internally, staff believe the new signing can both relieve pressure on Casemiro and, in certain matches, line up alongside the Brazilian to form a rugged shield.

Ten Hag said: “We needed more balance and more options in that area. Manuel reads the game very well, he covers large spaces and he brings a relentless attitude without the ball. On the ball he is calm, he connects lines, and he is always looking for ways to move us forward. These are qualities that can lift the entire side.”

Sources indicate that United’s data analysts highlighted Ugarte’s ball-winning numbers and ability to shut down counterattacks as elite. His pressing figures in France were among the very highest in the league, while his anticipation and sharp reactions drew frequent praise from coaches who worked with him. One member of United’s recruitment unit described him as “a player who treats every duel like a final”.

The move also signals a stylistic shift for United. Last season, Ten Hag’s side often lacked control in central areas, especially against strong rivals. Ugarte’s arrival is seen as vital to addressing that flaw. Club insiders speak of a desire to create a side that can squeeze rivals higher up the pitch, force turnovers and sustain waves of pressure, rather than rely on sporadic counterattacks.

Supporters gathered outside Old Trafford on Friday evening, some still in work clothes, others draped in red and white, hoping to glimpse the new arrival. A small cheer went up when club media channels released the first images of Ugarte holding the shirt, bearing the number that will soon be sung on the terraces.

Among the crowd was Diego Silva, a Uruguayan who has lived in Manchester for more than a decade. “For us, this is huge,” he said, proudly wearing his national team jersey. “Manuel is the kind of player people back home love. He runs, he tackles, he never hides. At PSG maybe he didn’t always get the credit he deserved. Here, if he brings that same energy, the supporters will adore him.”

Inside the club shop, young fans pressed their faces to screens replaying clips of his snarling challenges and crisp forward passes. Staff reported a surge in jersey orders within hours of the deal being confirmed, with many choosing to add Ugarte’s name even before he walks out at Old Trafford for the first time.

For Ugarte, this switch marks another step in a career that has moved rapidly. After emerging in Montevideo, he travelled to Europe as a teenager, rising quickly through the ranks in Portugal before earning a high-profile move to France. Now he arrives in England burdened with both a significant fee and the hope that he can anchor a new-era United.

Friends say he has remained grounded throughout each move. One former youth mentor in Uruguay described him as “obsessed with improvement, not fame”, recounting how Ugarte would stay long after team training to work on passing angles or recovery runs. Those habits, United believe, will help him cope with the glare that comes with life at one of the sport’s most scrutinised institutions.

There are, of course, challenges ahead. The pace and physical strain of the Premier League can unsettle even gifted newcomers, and competition for places in United’s midfield will be fierce. Behind the scenes, staff have prepared a tailored integration plan that includes language support, detailed analysis sessions and gradual increases in game minutes if required.

Ten Hag, though, sounds confident. “Any player who comes here needs time to adapt,” he said. “But Manuel has shown throughout his career that he learns fast. What matters most is his mentality. He wants to work, he wants to listen, he wants to improve. With that attitude, and with the support of our group and our supporters, I am sure he will have a big impact.”

Ugarte, who was due to link up with his new teammates over the weekend, had already begun studying United’s recent matches before the deal was finalised. Those close to him say he has been particularly focused on understanding the movements of Bruno Fernandes and Kobbie Mainoo, eager to anticipate where they like to receive the ball and how he can best serve them.

“I know this club carries an incredible history,” he said in an interview with club media. “But for me, history is also a responsibility. We must honour it every day. That is why I am here – to give everything, to compete for every ball, and to help bring joy back to our supporters. I have dreamed of these nights since I was a child. Now it is time to work.”

As the lights dimmed around the stadium and supporters drifted into the damp Manchester evening, there was a sense that United’s summer plan was finally taking coherent shape. Whether Ugarte proves to be the missing anchor in Ten Hag’s evolving side will only become clear in the months ahead. For now, he has brought fresh hope, a fierce promise to give his all, and the belief that United’s long search for control in the centre of the pitch may, at last, be nearing an end.

Any other questions?
